entry.evidence: it remains unknown what drove this rapid ice-margin retreat during the Early Holocene

steps.action: Posed the question of what drove rapid Early Holocene ice-margin retreat across the marine-based KNS forefield, which geologic data alone cannot constrain.
steps.quote: it remains unknown what drove this rapid ice-margin retreat during the Early Holocene

steps.action: Framed two rival drivers, atmospheric forcing through surface mass balance and marine forcing through calving and ocean melt, to be tested with a calving-capable high-resolution model.
steps.quote: to specifically address how Holocene ice retreat across the KNS forefield was influenced by marine and atmospheric forcings

steps.action: Summarized the published radiocarbon and 10Be chronology of Holocene deglaciation in the KNS region, which shows rapid, synchronous retreat of landscape and fjords (Weidick 2012; Larsen 2014; Young 2021).
steps.quote: Collectively, the radiocarbon and 10 Be ages suggest rapid and synchronous deglaciation of both the landscape and fjord systems

steps.action: Configured a regional ISSM higher-order thermomechanical model on an anisotropic mesh refined to 1 km in fjords, with five vertical layers, quadratic vertical elements and an enthalpy formulation, following the authors' earlier setups.
steps.quote: the horizontal mesh resolution varies from 1 km in fjords

steps.action: Inferred the basal friction coefficient under present-day ice by inversion against satellite surface velocities, and parameterized it by bedrock elevation for ice-free areas.
steps.quote: using inverse methods (Morlighem et al., 2010; Larour et al., 2012) that satisfies the best match between modeled and satellite-derived surface velocities

steps.action: Added level-set ice-front tracking and von Mises stress calving, with stress thresholds of 600 kPa (grounded) and 200 kPa (floating) chosen within published ranges.
steps.quote: To simulate calving, we rely on the physically based Von Mises stress calving (Morlighem et al., 2016)

steps.action: Took high and low end-member temperature and precipitation histories from the Badgeley et al. (2020) data-assimilation reanalysis as climate forcing, with SMB computed by a PDD scheme.
steps.quote: This reanalysis relies on a data assimilation framework that combines the information from ice core proxies with climate-model simulations

steps.action: Designed a factorial experiment of four climate combinations, each run with calving on and with calving off (40 m/yr sub-shelf melt), plus later sensitivity runs.
steps.quote: We perform four transient model simulations using four combinations of possible climate scenarios shown in Table 1.

steps.action: Spun up each model under constant 12.4 ka climate for 20,000 years without calving, imposed boundary conditions from Briner et al. (2020), then ran each transiently from 12.4 ka to 2013 CE.
steps.quote: Each model is then run transiently through time from 12 400 years ago to 1850 CE

steps.action: Compared simulated deglaciation ages with the geologic ages: terrestrial surfaces deglaciate millennia before fjords, terrestrial timing barely differs between calving on and off, and higher precipitation delays retreat.
steps.quote: there is little difference between the age of deglaciation on terrestrial surfaces for simulations that allow

steps.action: Plotted simulated deglaciation age against elevation and found no elevational dependence, matching the geologic data.
steps.quote: In general, our simulations agree with the geologic data, indicating that there was no elevational dependence on the age of deglaciation

steps.action: Compared simulated ice-volume minima and minimum extents with relative sea-level and lake-sediment constraints; no run captures the timing of the minimum, and high-temperature runs fit best.
steps.quote: None of our simulations accurately capture the exact timing of the GrIS minimum in the KNS region

steps.action: Rejected both low-temperature forcing scenarios because their continued Holocene mass loss is inconsistent with the geologic and relative sea-level records.
steps.quote: Both low-temperature scenarios are inconsistent with the geological record as both show continued ice mass loss through the Holocene.

steps.action: Contrasted the calving-on and calving-off runs for 12-10 ka: calving speeds fjord flow by more than 200 m/yr, propagates thinning inland and reduces interior thickening and mass.
steps.quote: ice velocity differences for simulations with and without calving are in excess of 200 m yr - 1 along many fjords

steps.action: Compared simulated Early Holocene interior thickening with ice-core elevation records (Vinther 2009): calving-on runs (<120 m) fit the 30-70 m better than calving-off runs (>200 m).
steps.quote: our simulations that allow calving display inland thickening ( < 120 m) over the time interval 12–10 ka that is more consistent with thickening

steps.action: Reran the high-precipitation cases with a 1 MPa grounded-ice calving threshold and with a 120 m/yr sub-shelf melt rate; ice volume was unchanged or minimally changed.
steps.quote: adjusting the stress threshold from 600 kPa to 1 MPa has no effect on the evolution of the simulated ice volume

steps.action: Defended the calving auxiliary, which omits frontal melt and undercutting, by its low stress threshold and the insensitivity to 1 MPa, assuming undercutting would be negligible.
steps.quote: we cautiously assume that implementation of undercutting would have a negligible effect on the calving rates

steps.action: Kept the claim that terrestrial retreat was SMB-driven and best fit by warmer reconstructions, while calving strongly controlled regional ice volume change.
steps.quote: the terrestrial ice retreat is more sensitive to the SMB, with warmer climate reconstructions providing the best fit between the modeled and observed ice retreat

end.claim: Early Holocene terrestrial ice retreat across the KNS forefield was driven mainly by surface mass balance under warming and was insensitive to fjord calving, whereas calving strongly increased regional ice mass loss and inland thinning.

decisive_move.sentence: Pairing every climate scenario with calving-on and calving-off runs isolates the marine contribution; without this paired design neither the insensitivity of terrestrial retreat nor the calving control on mass loss could be stated.

gates.evidence: The atmospheric-versus-marine framing directed the calving on/off experimental design (§1 ¶4, §3.4 ¶1). The geologic data were all pre-existing and were not acquired under the hypothesis. The simulations were compared against geologic ages, RSL records and ice cores, and some scenarios failed (low-temperature runs rejected, §4.2 ¶5; no run captured the timing of the minimum). The insensitivity of terrestrial retreat to calving is a model-internal contrast, not a test against data. Nothing is stated as fixed before the comparison.

novelty_claims.quote: While our past ice flow modeling efforts excluded ice–ocean interactions (Briner et al., 2020), our simulations presented here take advantage of the recent implementation
[...] provides a foundation for future experiments using ISSM to simulate the influence of ice–ocean interactions

limits: No peer-review file or discussion was supplied, so no review sequence was coded; the review statement only names the editor and referees. The paper makes no explicit 'first' claim; the novelty entries are implicit (inference). Sub-claims and statuses: calving-on runs fit the ice-core thickening better (best_explanation); warmer reconstructions fit the terrestrial retreat best (best_explanation); the calving-driven velocity and thinning mechanism is a model-internal result not tested against data (none). The timing of the Holocene minimum was not reproduced by any run (none), and all runs end with a present-day margin too far west, a misfit left unquantified. The sensitivity analysis is partial: only two scenarios and one alternative value per parameter, and a full uncertainty analysis was declined for computational cost. The negligible effect of undercutting is an assumption inferred from the threshold test, not tested. GIA and RSL feedbacks were omitted and justified by citation (Caron 2018; Kajanto 2020). Internal inconsistencies: the Figure 12 caption cites 6 kPa where the text gives 600 kPa; §5.3 ¶2 cites Fig. 11 for the sensitivity tests shown in Fig. 12; the Figure 7 caption refers to Figs. 8 and 9 for the 12-10 ka analysis shown in Figs. 9 and 10. The composition is coded trace_series with reservations (inference): conditions are set in the model, not found, but the claim rests on the best fit against several independent geologic traces.

disagreements.target: Ice sheet models simulating 20-40 km retreat inboard of the present margin (Tarasov and Peltier, 2002; Lecavalier et al., 2014)
disagreements.support: Cited RSL and lake-sediment constraints indicating a minimal eastward retreat, together with this paper's best-fitting high-temperature runs, which reach minima close to the present margin.
disagreements.quote: as simulated by some ice sheet models in this sector (20–40 km; Tarasov and Peltier, 2002; Lecavalier et al., 2014) is likely too extreme

disagreements.target: Coarse-resolution paleo-ice-flow models that do not resolve fjords
disagreements.support: The calving-on/off contrast at 1 km fjord resolution shows a strong calving control on ice volume that coarse grids cannot capture.
disagreements.quote: paleo-ice-flow models that do not sufficiently resolve fjord geometry may not capture dynamic processes

disagreements.target: The authors' prior modeling that excluded ice-ocean interactions (Briner et al., 2020)
disagreements.support: Adding calving leaves terrestrial retreat nearly unchanged but substantially changes ice mass loss and interior thinning.
disagreements.quote: While our past ice flow modeling efforts excluded ice–ocean interactions (Briner et al., 2020)
